blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — continuous IV insulin in severe DKA
stem: A critically ill adult with severe diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is receiving a continuous intravenous infusion of regular human insulin. Which statement best reflects current treatment guidance?

options.A: Continuous IV insulin is appropriate for severe DKA using a validated protocol, with frequent glucose and potassium assessment as insulin therapy and ketoacidosis correction proceed.
options.B: Uncomplicated mild DKA requires the same continuous IV insulin strategy in an intensive care setting because subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin is not an accepted treatment approach.
options.C: Potassium surveillance can be reduced once IV insulin begins because insulin correction of ketoacidosis does not meaningfully lower serum potassium or create hypokalemia risk.
options.D: Use of IV regular human insulin in severe DKA means subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin analogs are inappropriate for selected uncomplicated mild or moderate DKA cases.

rationale: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026 state that severe DKA is treated with continuous intravenous insulin using a fixed-rate or validated nurse-driven protocol. The same guidance notes that selected uncomplicated mild DKA can be managed with subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin, so IV therapy is not required for every DKA presentation. Current NOVOLIN R labeling requires close glucose and potassium monitoring during intravenous administration because hypoglycemia and hypokalemia can occur. Therefore A is correct. B overgeneralizes IV treatment to uncomplicated mild DKA, C ignores insulin-related potassium shifts, and D incorrectly excludes a guideline-supported subcutaneous approach for selected less severe DKA.
educational_objective: Recognize continuous IV insulin as appropriate for severe DKA while maintaining glucose and potassium monitoring and understanding that selected uncomplicated mild or moderate DKA may be treated with subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin under an appropriate protocol.
source_organization: American Diabetes Association (ADA); DailyMed / FDA labeling
source_document_title: 16. Diabetes Care in the Hospital: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026; NOVOLIN R (insulin human) injection — Full Prescribing Information
source_version_date: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, published 2026; current NOVOLIN R labeling accessed 2026-08-26
source_locator: ADA 2026 Section 16, DKA/HHS management: severe DKA — continuous IV insulin with fixed-rate or validated nurse-driven protocol; uncomplicated mild DKA may use subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin every 1-2 hours. NOVOLIN R §2.2 Intravenous Administration: administer IV under medical supervision with close monitoring of blood glucose and potassium to reduce hypoglycemia and hypokalemia risk.
source_claim_supported: Severe DKA is appropriately managed with continuous IV insulin under a validated protocol; selected uncomplicated mild DKA can use subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin; IV regular insulin requires close glucose and potassium monitoring.
blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: administer and monitor parenteral medications; evaluate medication response. Physiological Adaptation: manage acute metabolic emergencies.
candidate_reasons_resolved: Rewrote all four choices without absolute-word distractor cues.
Made each option a substantive DKA-management statement and preserved the severity-specific distinction supported by ADA 2026.
audit_note: Independent adversarial review confirms A uniquely reflects ADA 2026 severe-DKA guidance and IV insulin safety monitoring; no absolute-word cue or second defensible answer remains.
